readings.title: Kari the Elephant: the cobra and the jungle moon (chapter v)
readings.challenge: Separate what the narrator saw from the general rules he draws about animals, and notice when an adventure turns mysterious.
readings.focus: A fight with a cobra on a river bank, then a night when the jungle seems to call Kari away.
readings.context: Dhan Gopal Mukerji (1890–1936) grew up in a village near Calcutta, India, and wrote in English for young readers in America; Kari the Elephant (1922) was his first book. The narrator remembers caring for the young elephant Kari as a boy; Kopee is his pet monkey. Here they are travelling home after a visit to the city of Benares. A cobra is a poisonous snake that spreads a hood; an ankus is a hooked stick used to guide an elephant.
readings.contentNote: An elephant and the narrator kill a cobra. The narrator states beliefs about animals, including the jungle season “when elephants kill elephants to win their mates,” as facts.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “The Jungle Spirit,” the whole chapter; opens “It took us much longer to return home. We lost nearly twenty-four hours in a jungle where…”; closes “…even the knowledge that the moon was up could be vouched for in this thick black place.”.

questions.prompt: Kari squirts water at the monkey, and the narrator concludes, “This shows that elephants have a sense of humor.” What did he actually see, and is his conclusion justified?
facilitatorNotes: He saw Kari spray the monkey, who ran up and down the shore out of range. Humour is one explanation; play, or simply enjoying the water, are others. The narrator often turns one event into a rule about all elephants or all monkeys; readers can accept the story’s charm while noticing the leap.
evidence: This shows that elephants have a sense of humor.

questions.prompt: During the fight with the cobra, how do the elephant, the monkey and the boy each respond? Why does Kopee finally run only when the boy comes near with a stick?
facilitatorNotes: Kari pins the snake and keeps lifting his foot to strike its head; Kopee sits “hypnotized” with terror; the boy creeps round, then strikes. Kopee is freed the moment he sees “someone who could kill the snake,” and afterwards hides in a tree because he is ashamed. The narrator imagines the monkey’s feelings as if they were a person’s.
evidence: The spirit of terror that had held him hypnotized so long was broken at last, for he had seen someone who could kill the snake.
he was so ashamed of being afraid that he preferred to be alone in the privacy of the tree

questions.prompt: In the last paragraphs the chapter changes from adventure to something stranger. Which words make the night feel supernatural, and why might Kari plunge into the river?
facilitatorNotes: The “terrible face of the moon,” a moon “very rarely seen by men,” the “call of the summer” and white shapes that are “the spirits of the jungle” make the jungle feel alive with the dead. The narrator admits “no one ever knows.” Kari may be answering instinct (the season of challenge between elephants) or something the narrator can only call spiritual; the chapter leaves both open and ends in total darkness.
evidence: this was another moon, very rarely seen by men
These are the spirits of the jungle, the dead ancestors of the animals now living.

readings.title: Kari the Elephant: the flute and the man-eater (chapter vii, part 1 of 2)
readings.challenge: Sort the narrator’s claims into what he witnessed, what he was told and what he believes.
readings.focus: The boy learns to guide Kari with music, and a man-eating tiger brings a British official to the village.
readings.context: Since a night in the jungle when Kari fought a wild elephant and came home wounded, he has grown calm and fearless. Kopee is the narrator’s pet monkey. A stag is a male deer; a musk-deer is a small deer. During British rule in India, a magistrate was the British official in charge of a district.
readings.contentNote: A tiger kills cattle and a man. The narrator generalises freely about animals (“Monkeys have no brains”), and the passage refers to the British ban on Indians owning rifles.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “The Tiger Hunt,” from the opening through Kari’s trial under gunfire; opens “I have told you that Kari was not a hunting elephant. After that experience in the…”; closes “…never surprised. That shows that Kari's ancestors were undoubtedly very gentle elephants.”.

questions.prompt: The narrator makes several claims about music and animals. Which does he say he saw “with my own eyes,” and which are things people say?
facilitatorNotes: Snakes dancing to a flute and a flower put to sleep by a tune are stated as general beliefs (“There is supposed to be”). The deer coming out of the forest one by one is the scene he witnessed and describes in detail. Readers should notice the difference before trusting the general claims.
evidence: There is supposed to be a kind of flower, like a sensitive plant, that can be put to sleep by the playing of a very delicate tune.
I have seen with my own eyes how fond the deer are of music.

questions.prompt: How does the boy train Kari to follow his flute, and how long does it take? What does the contrast with Kopee show about the narrator?
facilitatorNotes: He searches for the few notes that make Kari stop and listen and slowly lengthens the time from a minute and a half to ten minutes, and after another year can guide him for days without a word. He dismisses Kopee with “Monkeys have no brains,” a hasty judgment of an animal that simply would not listen. His patience with Kari and impatience with the monkey both show his attachment to the elephant.
evidence: By the end of August, I could make Kari listen to my music for ten minutes at a time.

questions.prompt: Why must the village send for a British official? What do the narrator’s “rules by which men hunt in India” prepare us to expect?
facilitatorNotes: Under British rule Indians could not carry rifles, so the village depends on a foreign official to deal with a man-eater. The narrator describes him lightly as “chubby-faced” with a red face. The rules (never shoot a weaker animal, warn a tiger first, or “pay for it”) set up a test the hunt will apply.
evidence: In India the government does not allow the people to carry rifles of any sort
if you want to shoot a tiger or a leopard, you give it a warning. If you do not do so, you generally pay for it.

readings.title: Kari the Elephant: the tiger hunt (chapter vii, part 2 of 2)
readings.challenge: Follow fast action closely enough to decide who really saved whom.
readings.focus: A hunt goes wrong when a rule is broken, and a boy, an elephant and a flute save a British official.
readings.context: A man-eating tiger has been threatening the narrator’s village, and the British district magistrate has come to kill it, riding on Kari. The narrator can guide Kari by playing his flute. A howdah is a seat with sides fixed on an elephant’s back; beaters drive animals out of the forest towards the hunters; a cheetah is a spotted wild cat.
readings.contentNote: A tiger attacks the hunters, wounds the elephant and is shot at close range; the boy is splashed with its blood. The boy curses the official with an insult.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “The Tiger Hunt,” from the departure for the hunt to the end of the chapter; opens “After killing some more birds, the magistrate became quite convinced that Kari would do…”; closes “…they had skinned the tiger, they found its length to be nine feet, not counting the tail.”.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator describe the animals driven past the clearing? Choose one comparison and explain what it shows.
facilitatorNotes: Antelopes dash “like burnt gold flashing through emerald water”; a boar rushes “like a black javelin”; elephants pass silently “like walking cathedrals.” The comparisons give each animal its own speed, colour and dignity; the cathedral image makes the wild elephants solemn and huge, unlike the noisy rhinoceros.
evidence: like burnt gold flashing through emerald water

questions.prompt: Why is the boy so furious with the magistrate? What happens because the rule was broken?
facilitatorNotes: The magistrate fires at a half-seen tiger “without any warning” and only wounds its hind leg, so the enraged tiger attacks the howdah. The boy’s angry questions name the rule from earlier. A boy cursing a British official is startling; since they share no language, the magistrate probably does not understand, which adds a grim comedy.
evidence: Without any warning the magistrate fired
why did you not give him warning before you shot?

questions.prompt: Who saves the magistrate? Look at the last two sentences: what does the contrast between the Englishman and the boy suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Kari pulls down a branch to distract the tiger, and the boy controls his terror and strikes the tiger’s paw with his flute, which gives the magistrate time to fire. Afterwards the official measures his trophy while the boy searches for his broken flute. Readers may see a quiet criticism of the hunter, or simply two different things each one values.
evidence: I took my flute and hit the tiger's knuckles with it.
The Englishman went to see how big the tiger was while I led Kari in quest of my broken flute.
